Cyclone Idai - Mozambique

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
On 15 March the devastating cyclone Idai hit the Mozambique coast, killing more than a thousand people and leaving hundreds of thousands destitute.

Unique Selling Point:
We travel to Mozambique to get a first-hand account of the devastating effects of Cyclone Idai. The city of Beira is said to be 90% destroyed and rescue efforts continue to help people affected by the intense storm that hit the coast on 15 March. Rescue SA and Gift of the Givers are on site, providing food and shelter for the homeless, and every day more and more people are picked up from roofs and trees in the low-lying rural areas around Beira.

Summary:
Winds of up to 170 kph (105 mph) and flooding swept across southeastern Africa, including Zimbabwe and Mozambique, affecting more than 2.6 million people, United Nations officials said on Tuesday. Eye-witnesses have said that it looked like the town of Beira was hit by a Tsunami. There are reports of pets being swept away by the strong winds, and people killed by flying debris. Official numbers from the Red Cross is more than 400,000 homeless, although people on the ground says it's more than double that.

Further information:
Intense Tropical Cyclone Idai is regarded as one of the worst tropical cyclones on record to affect Africa and the Southern Hemisphere as a whole.

Script:


CYCLONE IDAI




V/O
On the night of Thursday 14 March, a tropical cyclone - equivalent to a stage 3 hurricane - hit the east coast of Mozambique, working it's way into Zimbabwe. With the official death toll standing close to a thousand people, rescue agencies from across the globe are working tirelessly to get aid to the worst affected.
LINK
Even though climatologists knew DAYS in advance, governments issued the necessary warnings to public and international rescue organisations were on stand-by, no-one was prepared for the scale of destruction Cyclone Idai would leave behind.
Paul Herbst
The initial intel from disaster management said Beira was going to be the worst hit. When we arrived there it was catastrophic. It was really bad.
V/O
Paul Herbst was one of the first rescuers to reach Mozambique after Idai hit.
Paul Herbst
We honestly thought there would be some flooding in selected areas, but when we arrived there and we saw the flood plains and the amount of water it was 100x worse than what we thought.
V/O
The cyclone made landfall in central Mozambique, near the port city of Beira, with an estimated population of a half a million. Local taxi driver, Antonio Renço says the winds started coming in strong over the ocean at around 8pm that night.
ANTONIO RENÇO
The wind was from this way to the houses, first wind until 11 o'clock tonight. They stop.
V/O
The eye of the storm passed over Beira just before midnight and then the second wave hit.
Antonio
The second one, it was very very strong. Destroyed many houses. The people died.
V/O
The city was devastated. Trees uprooted, homes destroyed. Streets and buildings were flooded. Thousands of people lost everything.
Antonio
All of them was saying Jesus, Jesus. All my life I never seen something like this.
V/O
The city was cut off from the world, literally an island in a sea of water. It was only when the airport reopened three days later that the bulk of the aid and rescuers started arriving.
LiNK
It's Day 8 after Cyclone Idai ravaged Beira. The city is still without water and electricity and ATMs only started operating yesterday. But clean-up operations are well underway.
V/O
Driving around Beira it is clear that almost no building was left untouched. And as the rain continues, people navigate their way through puddles of mud and rubbish, trying to find drinkable water and food.
Antonio
We don't have electricity, we don't have water. This is the first problem. The second one is food. The shops the food is very expensive, the people don't have money.
V/O
These rice silos were crumpled by the wind, and with the influx of people to the city, food and bottled water is becoming increasingly hard to find. Some tanks with potable water have been made available in the city but it's not enough. Of particular concern is the many people drinking stormwater, and that the first cases of waterborne diseases have already been reported.
Antonio
To eating yesterday he get some fish from the sea, and then he cooking only fish. They're eating only fish. There is nothing to eat. Inside, nothing for sleeping....
V/O
This family was lucky to escape with minor injuries, but their home was completely destroyed. The newly built corrugated iron shack will have to do for the weeks - and possibly months - to come...
LINK
The settlement I'm in is called Priya Nova and this area was hit particularly hard because of it's close proximity to the beach not too far away. People are already rebuilding and trying to pick up the pieces of their lives but to give you an indication of how powerful Idai was, behind me is a cellphone tower that was blown over.
V/O
Along with the heavy rains and winds of up to 200kms/h came tsunami-like waves from the ocean...
Antonio
There started rain and wind but 9pm there started water from the sea/beach.
V/O
Jose and his family were in their little concrete-walled house, trying to hold on to the little they have.
Antonio
He says the family when it starts, the one was with a stick to make sure if it's coming down you can hold it up. The other ones took this to put it on their hair.
V/O
Along the beach you see people salvaging rubble that might end up being useful for rebuilding... people filling sandbags to try and stop the water from running into their homes. According to the Red Cross about 90% of Beira was destroyed by the cyclone. Once popular tourist restaurants lie in ruins along the coastline.
Antonio
Ive been here two times.... Very very nice...

It was beautiful that restaurant, beautiful in town. But now, one week – it's gone.
V/O
The amount of sand that washed ashore is a good indication of the power of the waves from the sea.
Daniel
The roof is gone, all water is here.
V/O
Hotel owner Daniel Nitin now relies on a generator to try and accommodate some guests at his establishment.
Daniel
The big problem is the electricity because the water goes inside the box of the light. That's why many lights, when I make start, is gone.... But we are lucky, I say we are lucky because thank God we are alive. You know...
V/O
Rebuilding, he says will be a long and slow process but he is grateful that he and his family are still together. Others have not been so fortunate...
V/O
Outside Beira, hundreds of villages were scattered along the floodplain and their remoteness has made rescue efforts very challenging, says Gift of the Givers Team Leader, Ahmed Bham.
Ahmed GOTG
It's bad, the masses of water is not one of 5 or 10 kms, so villages you're flying across 30/40kms of water to reach those places. We need the water to recede so you can reach them, you know.
V/O
What made matters worse in the case of Idai, is that the storm travelled through Mozambique to the Zimbabwe border where it lingered for 3 days, says Prof Francois Engelbrecht, a climatologist at the Wits Global Change Institute.
Francois
The system was able to produce extremely high rainfall totals over a very very large area.
V/O
This led to additional flash floods and mudslides, and masses of water flowing downstream, causing the major rivers through central Mozambique to overflow their banks.
Francois
We have reports of river levels being 6 metres higher than what they usually are. And of course many of the mozambican villages are along those river banks.

Vast areas to the West and South of Beira were completely submerged in flood waters and thousand of people were trapped on roofs and in trees, waiting to be airlifted to safety.
Paul Herbst
One initial incident, I think it was a 5-year old girl, that was on a rooftop of one of the houses that we rescued. It was believed after chatting to her through one of the NGO organisations she was there for 4 days, on the roof, through thunderstorms, lightning, basically the whole aftermath of the storm. Her entire family got washed away and she was the only one left on the roof.
V/O
For the past 2 weeks rescuers have been working around the clock to evacuate people from flooded villages. Volunteer-doctors are seeing to the injured and food and water is slowly starting to reach affected communities as the water recedes and roads become accessible again.
Ahmed GOTG
If you look out what's there, this is not a 1-week, 2-week, 1-month, 2-month story. This could be up to a whole year to get these communities up again.
Antonio
We have to be strong. This is what I'm saying if I find some people I'm saying we have to be strong. Everybody, we have to help. We have to help to organise our province.
V/O
In Beira, some of the displaced families are living in overcrowded school buildings. But even here the roof was blown away and conditions are difficult. When it's not raining it is sweltering hot and stench of urine is almost overwhelming. Amongst the chaos the Red Cross is at hand to try and enforce certain hygiene standards and to assist the people.
Antonio
He says it is for all the peoples, but the first thing is for cleaning...
V/O
Whilst some women are mopping up excess rain water, others are washing clothes and children. And in a corner on a balcony, lunch is being prepared.


V/O
Idai is said to be one of the worst tropical cyclones to hit Southern Africa in recorded history, and more than 1,85 million people are affected in some way, but climate change experts say storms like these are no longer once-in-a-lifetime events.
Francois
There is evidence of the number of intense tropical cyclones, so here we mean category 3 to category 5 hurricanes, increasing in frequency across the globe.
V/o
Because of warming temperatures, the likelihood of intense storms like these forming in the South-west Indian ocean is increasing, and evidence point to the fact that the storms bring heavier rainfall when they occur.
Francois
Even South Africa is not exempt of the devastating impacts of landfalling tropical cyclones and under climate change the potential for these systems making landfall at more southerly locations is there.
V/O
Tropical Cyclone Idai has highlighted countries like Mozambique's vulnerability to global warming... and former first lady, Graça Machel, believes Beira will go down in history as having been the first city to be completely devastated by climate change...
Antonio
We are poor. All the building is down. Where are we going to sleep? So we just leave everything with the god.




PROMO 1 11”
Cyclone Idai has been described as an unprecedented natural disaster, causing widespread devastation. Carte Blanche went to Beira to see – first hand – the destruction and the suffering of some of the worst affected communities.


PROMO 2 11”
Tropical cyclone, Idai has had a devastating effect across three countries. With extensive flooding, drinkable water is now a luxury – BUT how can outbreaks of waterborne diseases be prevented?


PROMO 3 11”
Some two weeks later, rescue and aid organisations are still working tirelessly to reach and assist the remote villages of central Mozambique that were devastated by the recent tropical cyclone, Idai.

metadata.Further information: Intense Tropical Cyclone Idai is regarded as one of the worst tropical cyclones on record to affect Africa and the Southern Hemisphere as a whole.
